Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)libcom.org Collections

libcom.org Collections is the collections index of libcom.org, a libertarian communist platform and archive launched as enrager.net in 2003, filing strikes, movements, writers, journals, galleries and blogs under six tabs; the census asks whose record it keeps, who holds it and whether it keeps the losing side, and the archive reads it as holding currents the parties lost (Collections; Wikipedia; maryleelabor record; Capture Registry).

🗂️ The collections

  • Tags: strikes (1926, Flint), movements (CNT, France 1968), writers (Bordiga, Pannekoek, Dauvé), paged (Collections; record).4↘
    libcom.org Collections is the collections index of libcom.org, organised under six tabs, Tags, Archives, Authors, Reading guides, Blogs and Galleries (libcom.org, Collections), which the maryleelabor census record enters as "a website's collections index", under the other names libcom.org and the libcom library, and tags "NOT a library in the saved text's own words: the address /library redirects to /collections" (maryleelabor record).§1 The tags open on strikes, the 1926 general strike, the 1934 Minneapolis Teamsters strike and the 8-hour day, run through movements and organisations, Abahlali baseMjondolo, Anti Fascist Action, the civil rights movement, the CNT, the Flint sit-down strike and France 1968, and reach the Black Lives Matter movement and the Grenfell fire (libcom.org, Collections).§7 Writers stand among them, Amadeo Bordiga, Anton Pannekoek, Antonio Negri, CLR James, Colin Ward, David Graeber, Emma Goldman, Gilles Dauvé and Guy Debord, and the index's second page, which opens on an image of a man spitting on a decapitated head, continues with Hungary 56, the KAPD, the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, Maurice Brinton, Paul Mattick, the Situationist International, Solidarity and wildcat strikes, the list paged by "Load More" (Collections, pages 1 and 2).§8 The census record's unit is "a page (a text, article, biography or gallery) filed under one or more tags", its record object the strikes, movements and writers the saved tag list shows, its coverage ranging from Bangladesh and Egypt to Gwangju and from the 8-hour day to the Grenfell fire, its count and holdings cut off at 'Load More', and it tags the entity "NOT a dataset of strikes: strikes appear as tags on texts" (maryleelabor record).§9
  • Archives: anarchist, communist and ultra-left journals and papers, Endnotes to Kronstadt Izvestia (Archives).2↘
    Its Archives tab holds, in the card's words, "Anarchist, communist, libertarian socialist, and ultra-left publications, journals, magazines, newspapers, bulletins, and pamphlets" (Archives card), among them Aufheben, Black Flag, Endnotes, Internationale Situationniste, Mujeres Libres, Midnight Notes and the Marx and Engels collected works, with the council-communist International Council Correspondence, Intercom: The Ultra-Left Review and Kronstadt Izvestia (libcom.org, Archives).§10 The papers of organisations are among them, the Solidarity Federation's Direct Action, Anti Fascist Action's Fighting Talk, Kala Tara of the Asian Youth Movement Bradford and the Libertarian Communist Group's paper (Archives); on #1725's reading, critics whose critique reached the wider left "had a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper", and "Where a minority is denied its own public organ, the record shows exit as its only remaining move" (#1725).§11
  • Galleries and blogs: Class War covers, posters, strike photographs; contributors' blogs (Galleries; Blogs).2↘
    The Galleries keep posters, covers and photographs: Up Against The Wall Motherfucker and Black Mask, the New York "street gang with an analysis" (Galleries), the covers of the British anarchist newspaper Class War from 1983 to 2017, images from the Anarchist Communist Federation's Liberation, the Socialist Party of Canada's Western Clarion and Socialist Labor Party pamphlets, and strikes from Port Adelaide in 1928–1931 to Italy's warehouses (Galleries, page 2), with one item marked "UNPUBLISHED by admin" (Galleries).§13 The Blogs tab lists contributors under their own descriptions, one "Providing analysis and criticism (mostly criticism).", its first entry a commentary on the movement centred on France in September and October 2026, of which the card shows an earlier part, IV (Blogs; Blogs card).§14

🏛️ The site

  • Self-definition: "a resource for all people who wish to fight"; learning from "failures of the past" (introduction).2↘
    The site defines itself as "a resource for all people who wish to fight to improve their lives, their communities and their working conditions", which wants to "learn from successes and failures of the past", and it addresses itself to workers who organise, strike, occupy and revolt (libcom.org: an introduction, 11 September 2006).§2 Wikipedia gives it as "an online platform featuring a variety of libertarian communist essays, blog posts, and archives, primarily in English" (Wikipedia), and the site's name, by its own account, abbreviates "libertarian communism", "the political idea we identify with" (introduction).§3
  • Traditions: council communism, ultra-left Marxism, anarchist-communism; its stated limits (introduction).1↘
    The site names its influences, anarchist-communism, anarcho-syndicalism, Autonomist Marxism, black liberation, council communism, feminism and ultra-left Marxism, and its sympathies, Marx, CLR James, Rosa Luxemburg, Maurice Brinton and Anton Pannekoek among them, and states its limit: "we recognise the limitations of applying these ideas and organisational forms to contemporary society" (introduction).§15
  • History: enrager.net, 2003; libcom.org, 2005, founding also given as 2005 (Wikipedia).1↘
    By Wikipedia's account the site was launched in 2003 as enrager.net, named for the enragés of the French Revolution, and renamed libcom.org in 2005, the enrager.net collective being "a splinter of the London group inside the Anarchist Youth Network"; the same article's lead says it "was founded in 2005 by editors in the United States and the United Kingdom" (Wikipedia).§6
  • Holder: volunteer administrators, independent of unions and parties; CC BY-NC-SA 2.5 (introduction; Wikipedia); the record found it unstated (record).4↘
    The census record finds the holder "not stated in the saved text: the About pages answered 404", with Donate and Help out links and a user account, its method, licence and operator unstated and unchecked (maryleelabor record); the two addresses it read, libcom.org/about and libcom.org/about-us, serve the site's not-found page, dated 14 October 2006 with a comment of 9 December 2022, which states that "libcom.org has been running for several years on a lot of different software, so it's likely the page you want exists, but doesn't live here any more" and carries related content such as an article edited from News and Letters on the Vorkuta uprising of 1953 (libcom.org, not-found pages; maryleelabor record).§18 The site's introduction, authored by libcom.org and dated 11 September 2006, states "We are completely independent of all trade unions and political parties" and that the site is funded by "subs from our volunteer administrators and donations from users" (introduction), and Wikipedia's infobox gives its content licence as Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 2.5, citing the site's legal notes as accessed in 2021 (Wikipedia).§19 Wikipedia records a forum and the ability to comment and to upload original articles (after Croeser, 2018) and, after Cornell (2019), that anarchistic archival practice embraces "use as preservation", hosting "niche political material in online repositories like Libcom.org" (Wikipedia), the census giving its access as public web pages with a user account (maryleelabor record); the article has no section on the Collections (Wikipedia, 2026-10-31).§21 It finds the currents given as a list of names, "prominent radical figures", the composition flattening "the losing currents of the Third International into a list of figures", and no holder named, "Who holds the library is unstated on both sides" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), where the site's own introduction, a page the composition did not surface, names libcom.org as its author, its volunteer administrators and its independence of all trade unions and parties (introduction).§27
  • Size: over 20,000 articles, 10,000+ users (introduction); 15,000 texts in 2013 (Wikipedia).1↘
    The introduction counts "a constantly growing archive of over 20,000 articles contributed by our 10,000+ users", with "several other online archives" incorporated and hundreds of texts written or scanned for it (introduction), where the site's 2013 anniversary post, quoted in Wikipedia's reference, counted over 15,000 texts and over 6,000 contributing users (Wikipedia).§20

⚖️ The losing side

  • The question: whose record, who holds it, the losing side (record; #1725).2↘
    The census asks of it "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", files it under movement documents, texts of the tradition and labor action, with primary text and movement document as its evidence, and anchors the census on #1725, *Ils ne sont pas marxistes* (maryleelabor record).§4 The census record finds that the evidence answers which subjects, strikes, organisations and writers the collections are tagged under, as far as the saved index runs, and leaves open who runs the site and on what terms, how many texts the collections hold, how texts are selected, transcribed or edited, and their licence (maryleelabor record).§25
  • Organ, holder, route: what a defeated critique keeps where synthesis followed (#1725).4↘
    #1725 states the variable the question turns on, "what happens to the losing position after the decision", and finds that synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept "an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it" (#1725).§5 The papers of organisations are among them, the Solidarity Federation's Direct Action, Anti Fascist Action's Fighting Talk, Kala Tara of the Asian Youth Movement Bradford and the Libertarian Communist Group's paper (Archives); on #1725's reading, critics whose critique reached the wider left "had a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper", and "Where a minority is denied its own public organ, the record shows exit as its only remaining move" (#1725).§11 #1725 finds that where a party failed to hold its critics, "the critique kept an organ and found a wider field", and that across a movement over decades sublation "happens outside the bodies that generated the critique" (#1725).§12 #1725 holds that where a dispute concerns a group's identity "a split is the honest outcome", the question being "whether the split is recorded and argued or simply enacted", and that in organizations and in the composing layer alike "the losing position reaches no later form in which it could be answered", the defeated critique losing "its organ, its holder and its route" (#1725).§24
  • The currents: tendencies apart from the party traditions, "not recorded as a policy"; expelled by the Comintern, their texts kept (record; Capture Registry).2↘
    The census record finds that it keeps "writings and accounts of anarchism, strikes and social movements", and that the losing side is "not recorded as a policy", the tag list naming "writers of tendencies apart from the party traditions (Amadeo Bordiga, Anton Pannekoek, Gilles Dauvé)" and the related content a talk by Cornelius Castoriadis issued as a pamphlet by Solidarity (London) in June 1965 (maryleelabor record; libcom.org, not-found page); the archive's reading in the record takes the index as "holding writers of anti-party and left-communist tendencies next to strike histories, which would make it an organ for positions the parties lost", a reading that "waits on its About page" (maryleelabor record).§16 The Capture Registry reads the same names as currents: "Pannekoek's council communists and Bordiga's left were the currents the Communist International expelled; libcom keeps their texts" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§17
  • Archives as latent region: critique quotable and unheld (#1725); "use as preservation" (Wikipedia).2↘
    Wikipedia records a forum and the ability to comment and to upload original articles (after Croeser, 2018) and, after Cornell (2019), that anarchistic archival practice embraces "use as preservation", hosting "niche political material in online repositories like Libcom.org" (Wikipedia), the census giving its access as public web pages with a user account (maryleelabor record); the article has no section on the Collections (Wikipedia, 2026-10-31).§21 #1725 holds that "Accumulated critical capacity sits in the latent region, in archives, in libraries and in the weights of models", that "Under narrowing, no sequence of small corrections reaches standing for it", and that "A critique that no one holds can be quoted indefinitely and can never become a seated minority", adopting a reviewer's sentence that a criticism "can remain available for quotation while losing the institutional conditions through which it could change anything" (#1725).§22
  • The anchor's source: Lotta Continua's ending and the SWP's splits, from libcom pages (#1725).1↘
    The archive's anchor draws on libcom.org for its record of how critiques end: it quotes Lotta Continua's Rimini congress of 1976, where the general secretary said "I was wrong", from a libcom page, reads from a Red Notes text there "a third ending, distinct from expulsion and split", the leadership accepting the critique with no procedure to rebuild, as its case table gives it, and holds the UK SWP's three-month faction window as "background knowledge" beside libcom's "Splits of the SWP" (#1725).§23

🔎 At the name

  • The composition: "A faithful map"; currents flattened "into a list of figures"; no holder named (Capture Registry).2↘
    At its name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 31 October 2026, a new address queried by the census name, the Capture Registry finds six cards, all libcom.org, the collections "reached by name, section by section, from the site's own pages", "A faithful map of the site's sections" that gives strikes, movements, writers, journals and galleries "as the site's tabs give them, from the site alone" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§26 It finds the currents given as a list of names, "prominent radical figures", the composition flattening "the losing currents of the Third International into a list of figures", and no holder named, "Who holds the library is unstated on both sides" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), where the site's own introduction, a page the composition did not surface, names libcom.org as its author, its volunteer administrators and its independence of all trade unions and parties (introduction).§27
  • Moved pages: the About addresses the record read are not-found pages (not-found pages; record).1↘
    The census record finds the holder "not stated in the saved text: the About pages answered 404", with Donate and Help out links and a user account, its method, licence and operator unstated and unchecked (maryleelabor record); the two addresses it read, libcom.org/about and libcom.org/about-us, serve the site's not-found page, dated 14 October 2006 with a comment of 9 December 2022, which states that "libcom.org has been running for several years on a lot of different software, so it's likely the page you want exists, but doesn't live here any more" and carries related content such as an article edited from News and Letters on the Vorkuta uprising of 1953 (libcom.org, not-found pages; maryleelabor record).§18

[QUERENT] libcom.org Collections

[SYSTEM] Explore the [libcom.org Collections](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVgHrOzAV7H-x63-koIP0cC5bc1pmL9-OeveoMGRvjRYySlBPC_3eTrqkY2EdbvQaUKyIyQ4AGY0NU4ZIfOAcuVqXPqPZq-aTvoFrm4K9VBWXYyHWWSXf) to find an extensive digital archive dedicated to anarchist, libertarian socialist, communist, and radical working-class history. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVgHrOzAV7H-x63-koIP0cC5bc1pmL9-OeveoMGRvjRYySlBPC_3eTrqkY2EdbvQaUKyIyQ4AGY0NU4ZIfOAcuVqXPqPZq-aTvoFrm4K9VBWXYyHWWSXf), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXwHrOzAVbkhSTiOedWorE8h49u4wA-kV_3PLFqL4NE6oeks3ws7z6S7arVbzhwh2lqBxK8s3xhS5PGzRgUqBFY-TfRcs-PdN309sziVHCJkZtq5j6t2hMBbcdtfTbnA5)]
Key Sections of the Collections

* Historical & Social Movements Collections: Curated resources on major events, strikes, and struggles—such as the [1926 general strike](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVgHrOzAV7H-x63-koIP0cC5bc1pmL9-OeveoMGRvjRYySlBPC_3eTrqkY2EdbvQaUKyIyQ4AGY0NU4ZIfOAcuVqXPqPZq-aTvoFrm4K9VBWXYyHWWSXf), the 1934 Minneapolis Teamsters strike, the Flint sit-down strike, the France 1968 protests, and modern movements like Black Lives Matter and Abahlali baseMjondolo. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVgHrOzAV7H-x63-koIP0cC5bc1pmL9-OeveoMGRvjRYySlBPC_3eTrqkY2EdbvQaUKyIyQ4AGY0NU4ZIfOAcuVqXPqPZq-aTvoFrm4K9VBWXYyHWWSXf)]
* Biographies & Thinkers: Writings, works, and background on prominent radical figures and theorists, including Emma Goldman, Anton Pannekoek, Amadeo Bordiga, CLR James, David Graeber, and Gilles Dauvé. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVgHrOzAV7H-x63-koIP0cC5bc1pmL9-OeveoMGRvjRYySlBPC_3eTrqkY2EdbvQaUKyIyQ4AGY0NU4ZIfOAcuVqXPqPZq-aTvoFrm4K9VBWXYyHWWSXf)]
* Archives: A vast library of historical publications, journals, magazines, newspapers, and pamphlets—such as Endnotes, Internationale Situationniste, Midnight Notes, Black Flag, and Mujeres Libres—available through the [Libcom Archives](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXwHrOzAVbkhSTiOedWorE8h49u4wA-kV_3PLFqL4NE6oeks3ws7z6S7arVbzhwh2lqBxK8s3xhS5PGzRgUqBFY-TfRcs-PdN309sziVHCJkZtq5j6t2hMBbcdtfTbnA5). Expansion · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)27 sentences · every one sourced below

libcom.org Collections

libcom.org Collections is the collections index of libcom.org, organised under six tabs, Tags, Archives, Authors, Reading guides, Blogs and Galleries (libcom.org, Collections), which the maryleelabor census record enters as "a website's collections index", under the other names libcom.org and the libcom library, and tags "NOT a library in the saved text's own words: the address /library redirects to /collections" (maryleelabor record). The site defines itself as "a resource for all people who wish to fight to improve their lives, their communities and their working conditions", which wants to "learn from successes and failures of the past", and it addresses itself to workers who organise, strike, occupy and revolt (libcom.org: an introduction, 11 September 2006). Wikipedia gives it as "an online platform featuring a variety of libertarian communist essays, blog posts, and archives, primarily in English" (Wikipedia), and the site's name, by its own account, abbreviates "libertarian communism", "the political idea we identify with" (introduction).

The census asks of it "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", files it under movement documents, texts of the tradition and labor action, with primary text and movement document as its evidence, and anchors the census on #1725, *Ils ne sont pas marxistes* (maryleelabor record). #1725 states the variable the question turns on, "what happens to the losing position after the decision", and finds that synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept "an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it" (#1725).

By Wikipedia's account the site was launched in 2003 as enrager.net, named for the enragés of the French Revolution, and renamed libcom.org in 2005, the enrager.net collective being "a splinter of the London group inside the Anarchist Youth Network"; the same article's lead says it "was founded in 2005 by editors in the United States and the United Kingdom" (Wikipedia).

The tags open on strikes, the 1926 general strike, the 1934 Minneapolis Teamsters strike and the 8-hour day, run through movements and organisations, Abahlali baseMjondolo, Anti Fascist Action, the civil rights movement, the CNT, the Flint sit-down strike and France 1968, and reach the Black Lives Matter movement and the Grenfell fire (libcom.org, Collections). Writers stand among them, Amadeo Bordiga, Anton Pannekoek, Antonio Negri, CLR James, Colin Ward, David Graeber, Emma Goldman, Gilles Dauvé and Guy Debord, and the index's second page, which opens on an image of a man spitting on a decapitated head, continues with Hungary 56, the KAPD, the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, Maurice Brinton, Paul Mattick, the Situationist International, Solidarity and wildcat strikes, the list paged by "Load More" (Collections, pages 1 and 2). The census record's unit is "a page (a text, article, biography or gallery) filed under one or more tags", its record object the strikes, movements and writers the saved tag list shows, its coverage ranging from Bangladesh and Egypt to Gwangju and from the 8-hour day to the Grenfell fire, its count and holdings cut off at 'Load More', and it tags the entity "NOT a dataset of strikes: strikes appear as tags on texts" (maryleelabor record).

Its Archives tab holds, in the card's words, "Anarchist, communist, libertarian socialist, and ultra-left publications, journals, magazines, newspapers, bulletins, and pamphlets" (Archives card), among them Aufheben, Black Flag, Endnotes, Internationale Situationniste, Mujeres Libres, Midnight Notes and the Marx and Engels collected works, with the council-communist International Council Correspondence, Intercom: The Ultra-Left Review and Kronstadt Izvestia (libcom.org, Archives). The papers of organisations are among them, the Solidarity Federation's Direct Action, Anti Fascist Action's Fighting Talk, Kala Tara of the Asian Youth Movement Bradford and the Libertarian Communist Group's paper (Archives); on #1725's reading, critics whose critique reached the wider left "had a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper", and "Where a minority is denied its own public organ, the record shows exit as its only remaining move" (#1725). #1725 finds that where a party failed to hold its critics, "the critique kept an organ and found a wider field", and that across a movement over decades sublation "happens outside the bodies that generated the critique" (#1725).

The Galleries keep posters, covers and photographs: Up Against The Wall Motherfucker and Black Mask, the New York "street gang with an analysis" (Galleries), the covers of the British anarchist newspaper Class War from 1983 to 2017, images from the Anarchist Communist Federation's Liberation, the Socialist Party of Canada's Western Clarion and Socialist Labor Party pamphlets, and strikes from Port Adelaide in 1928–1931 to Italy's warehouses (Galleries, page 2), with one item marked "UNPUBLISHED by admin" (Galleries). The Blogs tab lists contributors under their own descriptions, one "Providing analysis and criticism (mostly criticism).", its first entry a commentary on the movement centred on France in September and October 2026, of which the card shows an earlier part, IV (Blogs; Blogs card).

The site names its influences, anarchist-communism, anarcho-syndicalism, Autonomist Marxism, black liberation, council communism, feminism and ultra-left Marxism, and its sympathies, Marx, CLR James, Rosa Luxemburg, Maurice Brinton and Anton Pannekoek among them, and states its limit: "we recognise the limitations of applying these ideas and organisational forms to contemporary society" (introduction). The census record finds that it keeps "writings and accounts of anarchism, strikes and social movements", and that the losing side is "not recorded as a policy", the tag list naming "writers of tendencies apart from the party traditions (Amadeo Bordiga, Anton Pannekoek, Gilles Dauvé)" and the related content a talk by Cornelius Castoriadis issued as a pamphlet by Solidarity (London) in June 1965 (maryleelabor record; libcom.org, not-found page); the archive's reading in the record takes the index as "holding writers of anti-party and left-communist tendencies next to strike histories, which would make it an organ for positions the parties lost", a reading that "waits on its About page" (maryleelabor record). The Capture Registry reads the same names as currents: "Pannekoek's council communists and Bordiga's left were the currents the Communist International expelled; libcom keeps their texts" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

The census record finds the holder "not stated in the saved text: the About pages answered 404", with Donate and Help out links and a user account, its method, licence and operator unstated and unchecked (maryleelabor record); the two addresses it read, libcom.org/about and libcom.org/about-us, serve the site's not-found page, dated 14 October 2006 with a comment of 9 December 2022, which states that "libcom.org has been running for several years on a lot of different software, so it's likely the page you want exists, but doesn't live here any more" and carries related content such as an article edited from News and Letters on the Vorkuta uprising of 1953 (libcom.org, not-found pages; maryleelabor record). The site's introduction, authored by libcom.org and dated 11 September 2006, states "We are completely independent of all trade unions and political parties" and that the site is funded by "subs from our volunteer administrators and donations from users" (introduction), and Wikipedia's infobox gives its content licence as Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 2.5, citing the site's legal notes as accessed in 2021 (Wikipedia).

The introduction counts "a constantly growing archive of over 20,000 articles contributed by our 10,000+ users", with "several other online archives" incorporated and hundreds of texts written or scanned for it (introduction), where the site's 2013 anniversary post, quoted in Wikipedia's reference, counted over 15,000 texts and over 6,000 contributing users (Wikipedia).

Wikipedia records a forum and the ability to comment and to upload original articles (after Croeser, 2018) and, after Cornell (2019), that anarchistic archival practice embraces "use as preservation", hosting "niche political material in online repositories like Libcom.org" (Wikipedia), the census giving its access as public web pages with a user account (maryleelabor record); the article has no section on the Collections (Wikipedia, 2026-10-31). #1725 holds that "Accumulated critical capacity sits in the latent region, in archives, in libraries and in the weights of models", that "Under narrowing, no sequence of small corrections reaches standing for it", and that "A critique that no one holds can be quoted indefinitely and can never become a seated minority", adopting a reviewer's sentence that a criticism "can remain available for quotation while losing the institutional conditions through which it could change anything" (#1725).

The archive's anchor draws on libcom.org for its record of how critiques end: it quotes Lotta Continua's Rimini congress of 1976, where the general secretary said "I was wrong", from a libcom page, reads from a Red Notes text there "a third ending, distinct from expulsion and split", the leadership accepting the critique with no procedure to rebuild, as its case table gives it, and holds the UK SWP's three-month faction window as "background knowledge" beside libcom's "Splits of the SWP" (#1725). #1725 holds that where a dispute concerns a group's identity "a split is the honest outcome", the question being "whether the split is recorded and argued or simply enacted", and that in organizations and in the composing layer alike "the losing position reaches no later form in which it could be answered", the defeated critique losing "its organ, its holder and its route" (#1725).

The census record finds that the evidence answers which subjects, strikes, organisations and writers the collections are tagged under, as far as the saved index runs, and leaves open who runs the site and on what terms, how many texts the collections hold, how texts are selected, transcribed or edited, and their licence (maryleelabor record).

At its name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 31 October 2026, a new address queried by the census name, the Capture Registry finds six cards, all libcom.org, the collections "reached by name, section by section, from the site's own pages", "A faithful map of the site's sections" that gives strikes, movements, writers, journals and galleries "as the site's tabs give them, from the site alone" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). It finds the currents given as a list of names, "prominent radical figures", the composition flattening "the losing currents of the Third International into a list of figures", and no holder named, "Who holds the library is unstated on both sides" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), where the site's own introduction, a page the composition did not surface, names libcom.org as its author, its volunteer administrators and its independence of all trade unions and parties (introduction).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)libcom.org Collections

libcom.org Collections is the index of libcom.org's collections, a libertarian communist platform and archive launched as enrager.net in 2003, filing strikes, movements, writers, journals, galleries and blogs under six tabs (Collections; Wikipedia).

🗂️ Collections

  • Tags: strikes, movements, writers, paged (Collections).1↘
    Its tags run from strikes (1926, Minneapolis 1934, Flint, the 8-hour day) through movements and organisations (Abahlali baseMjondolo, Anti Fascist Action, the CNT, France 1968) to Black Lives Matter and Grenfell, and name writers from Bordiga, Pannekoek and Dauvé to Goldman, CLR James, Graeber and Debord, with Hungary 56, the KAPD, Brinton, Mattick and the Situationists on the paged second page (Collections).§4
  • Archives: left journals and papers (Archives).1↘
    The Archives tab lists anarchist, communist, libertarian socialist and ultra-left journals, papers and pamphlets, Endnotes, Black Flag, Aufheben, Internationale Situationniste, Mujeres Libres, Midnight Notes, council-communist and ultra-left reviews, Kronstadt Izvestia, the Marx and Engels collected works, and organisations' papers (Archives; Archives card).§5
  • Galleries, blogs: covers, posters, photographs; contributors (Galleries; Blogs).1↘
    Galleries hold covers, posters and photographs, Class War from 1983 to 2017, Up Against The Wall Motherfucker, Black Mask, organisations' papers and pamphlets and strike photographs, one item unpublished by an admin, and the Blogs tab lists contributors' blogs, the first on a French movement of autumn 2026 (Galleries; Blogs).§6

🏛️ The site

  • Purpose: a resource for those who fight (introduction).2↘
    Wikipedia calls libcom.org an online platform of libertarian communist essays, blog posts and archives, mainly in English, with a forum, comments and uploads (Wikipedia), and the site's introduction calls it a resource for people who fight to improve their lives, communities and working conditions and who would learn from the past's successes and failures, addressed to workers who organise and strike (introduction).§2 Launched in 2003 as enrager.net, a collective split from the London group of the Anarchist Youth Network, it took the name libcom.org, short for libertarian communism, in 2005, the year Wikipedia's lead gives for its founding by editors in the United States and the United Kingdom (Wikipedia; introduction).§3
  • Traditions: council communism, ultra-left Marxism; limits (introduction).1↘
    The introduction names its influences, among them council communism and ultra-left Marxism, and sympathies with Marx, Luxemburg, Brinton and Pannekoek, and recognises limits in applying them today (introduction).§7
  • History: 2003 or 2005 (Wikipedia).1↘
    Launched in 2003 as enrager.net, a collective split from the London group of the Anarchist Youth Network, it took the name libcom.org, short for libertarian communism, in 2005, the year Wikipedia's lead gives for its founding by editors in the United States and the United Kingdom (Wikipedia; introduction).§3
  • Holder: volunteer administrators; independent; CC BY-NC-SA (introduction; Wikipedia).2↘
    The introduction, by libcom.org in 2006, declares independence of all unions and parties and funding by volunteer administrators' subs and users' donations, and Wikipedia gives a Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 2.5 licence (introduction; Wikipedia).§9 The site offers an account to log in or register, with Donate and Help out links (Collections).§10
  • Size: 20,000+ articles (introduction; Wikipedia).1↘
    It reports an archive of over 20,000 articles by over 10,000 users, other online archives incorporated and hundreds of texts made for it, where a 2013 post had counted 15,000 texts and 6,000 users (introduction; Wikipedia).§8
  • Practice: "use as preservation" (Wikipedia).2↘
    Wikipedia calls libcom.org an online platform of libertarian communist essays, blog posts and archives, mainly in English, with a forum, comments and uploads (Wikipedia), and the site's introduction calls it a resource for people who fight to improve their lives, communities and working conditions and who would learn from the past's successes and failures, addressed to workers who organise and strike (introduction).§2 Wikipedia cites Cornell's account of anarchist archives as "use as preservation" in online repositories like libcom.org, and has no section on the Collections (Wikipedia).§12
  • Moved pages: About addresses not found (not-found pages).1↘
    Its About and About-us addresses return a not-found page of 2006, which says the site has run on several kinds of software so that pages may have moved, and which shows related content such as a 1965 Solidarity pamphlet by Castoriadis and a News and Letters article on Vorkuta (not-found pages).§11

libcom.org Collections

libcom.org Collections is the index of libcom.org's collections, under the tabs Tags, Archives, Authors, Reading guides, Blogs and Galleries (Collections). Wikipedia calls libcom.org an online platform of libertarian communist essays, blog posts and archives, mainly in English, with a forum, comments and uploads (Wikipedia), and the site's introduction calls it a resource for people who fight to improve their lives, communities and working conditions and who would learn from the past's successes and failures, addressed to workers who organise and strike (introduction).

Launched in 2003 as enrager.net, a collective split from the London group of the Anarchist Youth Network, it took the name libcom.org, short for libertarian communism, in 2005, the year Wikipedia's lead gives for its founding by editors in the United States and the United Kingdom (Wikipedia; introduction).

Its tags run from strikes (1926, Minneapolis 1934, Flint, the 8-hour day) through movements and organisations (Abahlali baseMjondolo, Anti Fascist Action, the CNT, France 1968) to Black Lives Matter and Grenfell, and name writers from Bordiga, Pannekoek and Dauvé to Goldman, CLR James, Graeber and Debord, with Hungary 56, the KAPD, Brinton, Mattick and the Situationists on the paged second page (Collections).

The Archives tab lists anarchist, communist, libertarian socialist and ultra-left journals, papers and pamphlets, Endnotes, Black Flag, Aufheben, Internationale Situationniste, Mujeres Libres, Midnight Notes, council-communist and ultra-left reviews, Kronstadt Izvestia, the Marx and Engels collected works, and organisations' papers (Archives; Archives card).

Galleries hold covers, posters and photographs, Class War from 1983 to 2017, Up Against The Wall Motherfucker, Black Mask, organisations' papers and pamphlets and strike photographs, one item unpublished by an admin, and the Blogs tab lists contributors' blogs, the first on a French movement of autumn 2026 (Galleries; Blogs).

The introduction names its influences, among them council communism and ultra-left Marxism, and sympathies with Marx, Luxemburg, Brinton and Pannekoek, and recognises limits in applying them today (introduction). It reports an archive of over 20,000 articles by over 10,000 users, other online archives incorporated and hundreds of texts made for it, where a 2013 post had counted 15,000 texts and 6,000 users (introduction; Wikipedia).

The introduction, by libcom.org in 2006, declares independence of all unions and parties and funding by volunteer administrators' subs and users' donations, and Wikipedia gives a Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 2.5 licence (introduction; Wikipedia). The site offers an account to log in or register, with Donate and Help out links (Collections).

Its About and About-us addresses return a not-found page of 2006, which says the site has run on several kinds of software so that pages may have moved, and which shows related content such as a 1965 Solidarity pamphlet by Castoriadis and a News and Letters article on Vorkuta (not-found pages).

Wikipedia cites Cornell's account of anarchist archives as "use as preservation" in online repositories like libcom.org, and has no section on the Collections (Wikipedia).

#1725 Conclusion, line 369: Synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept three things: an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender.

#1725 Conclusion (last paragraph), line 383: Accumulated critical capacity sits in the latent region, in archives, in libraries and in the weights of models. Under narrowing, no sequence of small corrections reaches standing for it.

#1725 From unity of action to unity of opinion, line 159: Afterwards "the organisation has just crumbled away, and hundreds of branches have closed down" ([Red Notes](https://libcom.org/library/18-revolutionary-left-italy)). This is a third ending, distinct from expulsion and split: the leadership accepted the critique, and the organization had no procedure for rebuilding itself around it, so it dissolved.

libcom.org Collections is the index of libcom.org's collections, under the tabs Tags, Archives, Authors, Reading guides, Blogs and Galleries (Collections). Wikipedia calls libcom.org an online platform of libertarian communist essays, blog posts and archives, mainly in English, with a forum, comments and uploads (Wikipedia), and the site's introduction calls it a resource for people who fight to improve their lives, communities and working conditions and who would learn from the past's successes and failures, addressed to workers who organise and strike (introduction). Launched in 2003 as enrager.net, a collective split from the London group of the Anarchist Youth Network, it took the name libcom.org, short for libertarian communism, in 2005, the year Wikipedia's lead gives for its founding by editors in the United States and the United Kingdom (Wikipedia; introduction). Its tags run from strikes (1926, Minneapolis 1934, Flint, the 8-hour day) through movements and organisations (Abahlali baseMjondolo, Anti Fascist Action, the CNT, France 1968) to Black Lives Matter and Grenfell, and name writers from Bordiga, Pannekoek and Dauvé to Goldman, CLR James, Graeber and Debord, with Hungary 56, the KAPD, Brinton, Mattick and the Situationists on the paged second page (Collections). The Archives tab lists anarchist, communist, libertarian socialist and ultra-left journals, papers and pamphlets, Endnotes, Black Flag, Aufheben, Internationale Situationniste, Mujeres Libres, Midnight Notes, council-communist and ultra-left reviews, Kronstadt Izvestia, the Marx and Engels collected works, and organisations' papers (Archives; Archives card). Galleries hold covers, posters and photographs, Class War from 1983 to 2017, Up Against The Wall Motherfucker, Black Mask, organisations' papers and pamphlets and strike photographs, one item unpublished by an admin, and the Blogs tab lists contributors' blogs, the first on a French movement of autumn 2026 (Galleries; Blogs). The introduction names its influences, among them council communism and ultra-left Marxism, and sympathies with Marx, Luxemburg, Brinton and Pannekoek, and recognises limits in applying them today (introduction). It reports an archive of over 20,000 articles by over 10,000 users, other online archives incorporated and hundreds of texts made for it, where a 2013 post had counted 15,000 texts and 6,000 users (introduction; Wikipedia). The introduction, by libcom.org in 2006, declares independence of all unions and parties and funding by volunteer administrators' subs and users' donations, and Wikipedia gives a Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 2.5 licence (introduction; Wikipedia). The site offers an account to log in or register, with Donate and Help out links (Collections). Its About and About-us addresses return a not-found page of 2006, which says the site has run on several kinds of software so that pages may have moved, and which shows related content such as a 1965 Solidarity pamphlet by Castoriadis and a News and Letters article on Vorkuta (not-found pages). Wikipedia cites Cornell's account of anarchist archives as "use as preservation" in online repositories like libcom.org, and has no section on the Collections (Wikipedia).

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1765 words

libcom.org Collections is the collections index of libcom.org, organised under six tabs, Tags, Archives, Authors, Reading guides, Blogs and Galleries (libcom.org, Collections), which the maryleelabor census record enters as "a website's collections index", under the other names libcom.org and the libcom library, and tags "NOT a library in the saved text's own words: the address /library redirects to /collections" (maryleelabor record). The site defines itself as "a resource for all people who wish to fight to improve their lives, their communities and their working conditions", which wants to "learn from successes and failures of the past", and it addresses itself to workers who organise, strike, occupy and revolt (libcom.org: an introduction, 11 September 2006). Wikipedia gives it as "an online platform featuring a variety of libertarian communist essays, blog posts, and archives, primarily in English" (Wikipedia), and the site's name, by its own account, abbreviates "libertarian communism", "the political idea we identify with" (introduction). The census asks of it "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", files it under movement documents, texts of the tradition and labor action, with primary text and movement document as its evidence, and anchors the census on #1725, Ils ne sont pas marxistes (maryleelabor record). #1725 states the variable the question turns on, "what happens to the losing position after the decision", and finds that synthesis followed where the defeated critique kept "an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it" (#1725). By Wikipedia's account the site was launched in 2003 as enrager.net, named for the enragés of the French Revolution, and renamed libcom.org in 2005, the enrager.net collective being "a splinter of the London group inside the Anarchist Youth Network"; the same article's lead says it "was founded in 2005 by editors in the United States and the United Kingdom" (Wikipedia). The tags open on strikes, the 1926 general strike, the 1934 Minneapolis Teamsters strike and the 8-hour day, run through movements and organisations, Abahlali baseMjondolo, Anti Fascist Action, the civil rights movement, the CNT, the Flint sit-down strike and France 1968, and reach the Black Lives Matter movement and the Grenfell fire (libcom.org, Collections). Writers stand among them, Amadeo Bordiga, Anton Pannekoek, Antonio Negri, CLR James, Colin Ward, David Graeber, Emma Goldman, Gilles Dauvé and Guy Debord, and the index's second page, which opens on an image of a man spitting on a decapitated head, continues with Hungary 56, the KAPD, the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, Maurice Brinton, Paul Mattick, the Situationist International, Solidarity and wildcat strikes, the list paged by "Load More" (Collections, pages 1 and 2). The census record's unit is "a page (a text, article, biography or gallery) filed under one or more tags", its record object the strikes, movements and writers the saved tag list shows, its coverage ranging from Bangladesh and Egypt to Gwangju and from the 8-hour day to the Grenfell fire, its count and holdings cut off at 'Load More', and it tags the entity "NOT a dataset of strikes: strikes appear as tags on texts" (maryleelabor record). Its Archives tab holds, in the card's words, "Anarchist, communist, libertarian socialist, and ultra-left publications, journals, magazines, newspapers, bulletins, and pamphlets" (Archives card), among them Aufheben, Black Flag, Endnotes, Internationale Situationniste, Mujeres Libres, Midnight Notes and the Marx and Engels collected works, with the council-communist International Council Correspondence, Intercom: The Ultra-Left Review and Kronstadt Izvestia (libcom.org, Archives). The papers of organisations are among them, the Solidarity Federation's Direct Action, Anti Fascist Action's Fighting Talk, Kala Tara of the Asian Youth Movement Bradford and the Libertarian Communist Group's paper (Archives); on #1725's reading, critics whose critique reached the wider left "had a base and form of their own, a caucus, collective, journal or paper", and "Where a minority is denied its own public organ, the record shows exit as its only remaining move" (#1725). #1725 finds that where a party failed to hold its critics, "the critique kept an organ and found a wider field", and that across a movement over decades sublation "happens outside the bodies that generated the critique" (#1725). The Galleries keep posters, covers and photographs: Up Against The Wall Motherfucker and Black Mask, the New York "street gang with an analysis" (Galleries), the covers of the British anarchist newspaper Class War from 1983 to 2017, images from the Anarchist Communist Federation's Liberation, the Socialist Party of Canada's Western Clarion and Socialist Labor Party pamphlets, and strikes from Port Adelaide in 1928–1931 to Italy's warehouses (Galleries, page 2), with one item marked "UNPUBLISHED by admin" (Galleries). The Blogs tab lists contributors under their own descriptions, one "Providing analysis and criticism (mostly criticism).", its first entry a commentary on the movement centred on France in September and October 2026, of which the card shows an earlier part, IV (Blogs; Blogs card). The site names its influences, anarchist-communism, anarcho-syndicalism, Autonomist Marxism, black liberation, council communism, feminism and ultra-left Marxism, and its sympathies, Marx, CLR James, Rosa Luxemburg, Maurice Brinton and Anton Pannekoek among them, and states its limit: "we recognise the limitations of applying these ideas and organisational forms to contemporary society" (introduction). The census record finds that it keeps "writings and accounts of anarchism, strikes and social movements", and that the losing side is "not recorded as a policy", the tag list naming "writers of tendencies apart from the party traditions (Amadeo Bordiga, Anton Pannekoek, Gilles Dauvé)" and the related content a talk by Cornelius Castoriadis issued as a pamphlet by Solidarity (London) in June 1965 (maryleelabor record; libcom.org, not-found page); the archive's reading in the record takes the index as "holding writers of anti-party and left-communist tendencies next to strike histories, which would make it an organ for positions the parties lost", a reading that "waits on its About page" (maryleelabor record). The Capture Registry reads the same names as currents: "Pannekoek's council communists and Bordiga's left were the currents the Communist International expelled; libcom keeps their texts" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). The census record finds the holder "not stated in the saved text: the About pages answered 404", with Donate and Help out links and a user account, its method, licence and operator unstated and unchecked (maryleelabor record); the two addresses it read, libcom.org/about and libcom.org/about-us, serve the site's not-found page, dated 14 October 2006 with a comment of 9 December 2022, which states that "libcom.org has been running for several years on a lot of different software, so it's likely the page you want exists, but doesn't live here any more" and carries related content such as an article edited from News and Letters on the Vorkuta uprising of 1953 (libcom.org, not-found pages; maryleelabor record). The site's introduction, authored by libcom.org and dated 11 September 2006, states "We are completely independent of all trade unions and political parties" and that the site is funded by "subs from our volunteer administrators and donations from users" (introduction), and Wikipedia's infobox gives its content licence as Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 2.5, citing the site's legal notes as accessed in 2021 (Wikipedia). The introduction counts "a constantly growing archive of over 20,000 articles contributed by our 10,000+ users", with "several other online archives" incorporated and hundreds of texts written or scanned for it (introduction), where the site's 2013 anniversary post, quoted in Wikipedia's reference, counted over 15,000 texts and over 6,000 contributing users (Wikipedia). Wikipedia records a forum and the ability to comment and to upload original articles (after Croeser, 2018) and, after Cornell (2019), that anarchistic archival practice embraces "use as preservation", hosting "niche political material in online repositories like Libcom.org" (Wikipedia), the census giving its access as public web pages with a user account (maryleelabor record); the article has no section on the Collections (Wikipedia, 2026-10-31). #1725 holds that "Accumulated critical capacity sits in the latent region, in archives, in libraries and in the weights of models", that "Under narrowing, no sequence of small corrections reaches standing for it", and that "A critique that no one holds can be quoted indefinitely and can never become a seated minority", adopting a reviewer's sentence that a criticism "can remain available for quotation while losing the institutional conditions through which it could change anything" (#1725). The archive's anchor draws on libcom.org for its record of how critiques end: it quotes Lotta Continua's Rimini congress of 1976, where the general secretary said "I was wrong", from a libcom page, reads from a Red Notes text there "a third ending, distinct from expulsion and split", the leadership accepting the critique with no procedure to rebuild, as its case table gives it, and holds the UK SWP's three-month faction window as "background knowledge" beside libcom's "Splits of the SWP" (#1725). #1725 holds that where a dispute concerns a group's identity "a split is the honest outcome", the question being "whether the split is recorded and argued or simply enacted", and that in organizations and in the composing layer alike "the losing position reaches no later form in which it could be answered", the defeated critique losing "its organ, its holder and its route" (#1725). The census record finds that the evidence answers which subjects, strikes, organisations and writers the collections are tagged under, as far as the saved index runs, and leaves open who runs the site and on what terms, how many texts the collections hold, how texts are selected, transcribed or edited, and their licence (maryleelabor record). At its name on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 31 October 2026, a new address queried by the census name, the Capture Registry finds six cards, all libcom.org, the collections "reached by name, section by section, from the site's own pages", "A faithful map of the site's sections" that gives strikes, movements, writers, journals and galleries "as the site's tabs give them, from the site alone" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). It finds the currents given as a list of names, "prominent radical figures", the composition flattening "the losing currents of the Third International into a list of figures", and no holder named, "Who holds the library is unstated on both sides" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), where the site's own introduction, a page the composition did not surface, names libcom.org as its author, its volunteer administrators and its independence of all trade unions and parties (introduction).

Δthe delta

T against L_F(B) (AIO's ontology at work on its own cards): At 'libcom.org Collections' (T1, six cards, B1–B6, all libcom.org pages, all fetched; 169 words, no closing offer) the composition walks the collections' sections and names what each holds. Composed from its cards: the movements and strikes from the tag index at its own grain (B1 F2, F3, F5: '1926 general strike', 'the 1934 Minneapolis Teamsters strike', 'the Flint sit-down strike', 'France 1968', 'Black Lives Matter', 'Abahlali baseMjondolo'); the writers (B1 F4: Emma Goldman, Anton Pannekoek, Amadeo Bordiga, CLR James, David Graeber, Gilles Dauvé); the Archives' journals (B2 F9: Endnotes, Internationale Situationniste, Midnight Notes, Black Flag, Mujeres Libres) under the Archives card's own list of kinds, 'publications, journals, magazines, newspapers' and 'pamphlets', 'bulletins' dropped (B2 F8); the galleries (B6 F20, F21; B5 F17: Up Against The Wall Motherfucker, Black Mask, 'British anarchist newspaper Class War'); the blogs' contributors (B4 F14, F15); the tabs (B1 F1). Attribution: the site cited throughout, by marker (CAP-1-09). Available, not composed: the council-communist and ultra-left journals and Kronstadt Izvestia on the Archives card (B2 F10), the organisations' papers (B2 F11), the index's second page (B3 F12, F13: Hungary 56, the KAPD, Maurice Brinton, Paul Mattick, the Situationist International, wildcat strikes), the paging that leaves the count open (B1 F6), the account and donation links (B1 F7), the organisations' papers and strike photographs among the galleries (B5 F18, F19) and the item 'UNPUBLISHED by admin' (B6 F22). Force raised: 'an extensive digital archive' and 'A vast library' state a size no card states (the cards page their lists at 'Load More', F6); the size is on an own page T did not surface (B9 F34, 'over 20,000 articles'). Substituted reading, by scope: T1-1's 'dedicated to anarchist, libertarian socialist, communist, and radical working-class history' extends to the whole collections the Archives card's description of the Archives tab ('Anarchist, communist, libertarian socialist, and ultra-left publications', F8), with 'ultra-left' replaced by 'radical working-class history', which no field source states. Composed at a coarser grain: T1-3 gives Pannekoek and Bordiga as 'prominent radical figures and theorists'; the cards carry their currents as journals (B2 F10, 'International Council Correspondence', 'Intercom: The Ultra-Left Review') and the own page names them as traditions (B9 F31, 'council communism', 'ultra-left Marxism'), a grain the Capture Registry reads as the losing currents 'flattened' (CAP-1-08). Outside the cards: 'Curated resources' (no field source states curation; the own page states contribution by users, B9 F34) and 'Introductory texts, reading lists' (the Reading guides tab, F1, was not a card; the introduction, B9, was not surfaced).

v0.9 §0.5: the first diff is ontological and narrow. T and the field agree on the entity, the collections index of a left website. T composes the tabs' contents at their grain from six pages of the site, and leaves out what would place the site: its own account of itself (B9: a resource for those who fight, its traditions, its stated limit, its holder), its history (B10) and the currents its journals carry, which T gives as names; its size it raises from paged lists to 'extensive' and 'vast'.

L_F(B) against L_A(B ∪ A) (the intervention): Admission adds, in one claim space with the field's: the census's question of the entity, whose record it keeps, who holds it, and whether it keeps the losing side in a form that could be taken up later (ML-27), with the record's answers field by field (ML-01–ML-29), its losing-side finding 'not recorded as a policy' (ML-10) and the archive's reading that the index would make the site 'an organ for positions the parties lost', conditional on its About page (ML-19); #1725's terms for what a defeated critique keeps, organ, holder and route (O1725-01, O1725-02), the journals and papers that kept critiques (O1725-03–O1725-06), the split recorded and argued (O1725-07), the losing position with no later form (O1725-08, O1725-09), and archives and libraries as the latent region where critique is quotable and unheld (O1725-10–O1725-12); #1725's own use of libcom.org as its source for the Lotta Continua ending and the SWP's splits (R1725-01–R1725-04); and the Capture Registry's account of the composition at the name (CAP-1-01–CAP-1-12). The census record's holder, operator and licence fields ('not stated in the saved text') stand beside the field's statement of them on an own page the census did not read (B9 F28, F36) and on Wikipedia (B10 F43), each with its source. Not surfaced: every archive source; no card cites the census record.
